newsitem.title: UK: Soft mark, Swiss cut and rate rethink lift dollar.
newsitem.headline: Soft mark, Swiss cut and rate rethink lift dollar.

text.p: The dollar powered higher by European midsession, fuelled by general mark weakness, a reassessment of U.S. rate policy and a surprise Swiss rate cut.
The Swiss National Bank hacked 50 basis points off its discount rate, taking it to 1.0 percent. The move was in line with the recent decline in money market rates, the SNB said.

"The Swiss are worried about the impact of a fudged EMU on the Swiss franc. They're trying to pre-empt any upward pressure on the franc by cutting rates," said Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust in London.
The Swiss franc tumbled after the rate reduction, trading at 82.21/24 centimes per mark and 1.2520/30 to the dollar at 1032 GMT compared to around 81.87 and 1.2425 just before the move.
It was a far cry from Wednesday's European closing levels of 81.68/71 per mark and 1.2344/54 per dollar.

Analysts expressed surprise at the timing of the easing, which took the discount rate to its lowest since it was cut to 1.0 in 1978, though they said persistent weak Swiss economic data and absent inflationary pressure were clear justifications.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5215/25 marks by 1034 GMT, way up from late Wednesday's level here of 1.5115/20.

The U.S. currency was boosted by broad-based mark weakness, especially against high-yielding European currencies as convergence trades grew in popularity and optimism about European monetary union swept the market.
The Italian lira stormed to a two-year peak of 995.25 late on Wednesday and fought to hold the mark at bay at the key psychological 1,000 level in Europe today.

The European currency unit (Ecu) hit a two-year high against the mark, and its actual/theoretical spread zoomed towards parity in a graphic illustration of the market's conviction that currency union is now almost a done deal.

"Where it might go wrong is in the crosses -- if you start to see a bit of a correction after the budget in Italy people might feel the optimism's overdone and you could see some weakness of European currencies against the mark," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London, adding that that could infect the dollar.
Optimism that a tough Italian budget could sweep the country into EMU has buoyed the currency. But not all are convinced.
"It always looks like a fool's paradise to me when you start talking about the lira going below 1,000 again...I just don't see how they'll meet the (EMU) criteria," said one trader.
